title: 24 Aug 2026 (Jeddah)
des: Saudi Prometric paediatrics recall, Jeddah, 24 August 2026

questions.question: A 3-year-old has an unsteady gait a week after a URTI. He is alert and CT brain is normal. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Post-infectious cerebellitis resolves over weeks.

questions.question: Which tool is used to assess level of consciousness in the PICU?
questions.exp: GCS (paediatric version for young children) assesses eye, verbal and motor responses.

questions.question: What is the typical length gain per month in the second 3 months of life?
questions.exp: About 3.5 cm/month in months 0-3 and 2 cm/month in months 3-6.

questions.question: A 4-month-old's head circumference has grown from 35 cm at birth to 47 cm; feeding is unchanged. What is the next investigation?
questions.exp: Rapid head growth across centiles suggests hydrocephalus.

questions.question: A 4-year-old has fever, a purpuric rash and neck stiffness. What is the most likely organism?
questions.exp: A purpuric rash with meningitis suggests meningococcus.

questions.question: A child with suspected meningococcal meningitis has GCS 10, normal BP and capillary refill 2 seconds. What is the next step?
questions.exp: Reduced consciousness (GCS ≤ 8-13 depending on guideline) is a contraindication to LP; antibiotics must not be delayed. The recall writer chose LP.
questions.d: Blood culture and immediate IV ceftriaxone, delaying LP

questions.question: What is the treatment of meningococcal meningitis?
questions.exp: Third-generation cephalosporin; give prophylaxis to close contacts.

questions.question: A boy with intellectual disability has a long face, large ears and large testes. What is the diagnostic test?
questions.exp: FMR1 repeat analysis.
questions.b: DNA analysis for FMR1 CGG repeats

questions.question: A girl with regression and stereotyped hand-wringing is assessed. Which test confirms the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Rett syndrome is an X-linked dominant MECP2 disorder.

questions.question: A toddler cries, holds his breath, turns blue and recovers quickly. What is the management?
questions.exp: Breath-holding spells are benign; check for iron deficiency.

questions.question: An infant has clusters of sudden extension of the head and arms, and EEG shows chaotic high-voltage spikes and waves. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Spasms can be flexor or extensor; hypsarrhythmia on EEG confirms West syndrome.

questions.question: A child has hard-to-control seizures, hypopigmented patches and developmental delay. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Ash-leaf macules, infantile spasms and cortical tubers.

questions.question: A child has bloody diarrhoea, petechiae, low platelets and high urea and creatinine. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: HUS: microangiopathic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and AKI, often after E. coli O157.

questions.question: A child develops encephalopathy and loss of bladder control after a diarrhoeal illness. What is the investigation?
questions.exp: Post-infectious ADEM or myelitis is seen on MRI.

questions.question: What is the typical outcome of parasagittal watershed injury in term HIE?
questions.exp: Watershed injury gives spastic quadriparesis.

questions.question: A child has acute leg weakness with hypertonia, hyperreflexia and a sensory level at the umbilicus. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: A sensory level localises to the cord (T10 at the umbilicus).

questions.question: A child has acute flaccid leg weakness with hyporeflexia but extensor plantars and urinary retention. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Early spinal shock causes flaccidity and areflexia, but Babinski and sphincter signs indicate the cord.

questions.question: Which MRI finding supports transverse myelitis?
questions.exp: MRI shows T2 hyperintensity with enhancement.
questions.c: Cord swelling with T2 signal and gadolinium enhancement

questions.question: A child with pneumonia on ceftriaxone is not improving and has a large effusion on ultrasound. What is next?
questions.exp: Enlarging or loculated effusions with respiratory compromise need drainage.

questions.question: A boy's father is 180 cm and mother 160 cm. What is his expected adult height range?
questions.exp: Boy: (father + mother + 13)/2 ± 8.5 cm. The recall writer recorded 166-180 for parents not stated.

questions.question: A child has episodic bitemporal headache with photophobia, abdominal pain and vomiting. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Paediatric migraine is often bilateral, with GI symptoms.

questions.question: A child loses consciousness immediately after head trauma and remains drowsy. Which bleed is more likely?
questions.exp: Immediate and persisting loss of consciousness favours subdural with diffuse injury; a lucid interval suggests extradural.

questions.question: A child is conscious after head trauma then becomes drowsy hours later. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Classic lucid interval from middle meningeal artery bleeding.

questions.question: A girl falls from a horse; neck X-ray is normal but she has slow breathing and cannot move her arm and leg. What is the investigation?
questions.exp: SCIWORA is common in children; MRI shows the cord injury.

questions.question: An 18-month-old's weight is 65% of expected for height, and height is 95% of expected for age. How is the nutritional state classified?
questions.exp: Waterlow: weight-for-height < 70% is severe wasting; height-for-age > 95% is not stunted. Figures were reconstructed.

questions.question: Parents are both carriers of an autosomal recessive disorder. What is the risk of an affected child?
questions.exp: 1 in 4 per pregnancy.

questions.question: A child has a focal seizure followed by transient weakness of the same side. What is the first investigation?
questions.exp: Todd paresis resolves within 48 hours; persistent deficit needs imaging.

questions.question: After an accident a child has bradycardia, gasping and GCS 5. What is the first step?
questions.exp: ABC order: airway with C-spine protection, then breathing, then circulation.
questions.a: Secure the airway and support breathing

questions.question: A child with sickle cell disease has septic arthritis. Which organism is particularly associated?
questions.exp: Salmonella is classic in SCD (Staph aureus is still common).

questions.question: A child with ataxia has recurrent chest infections and low IgA and IgG. Which test helps the diagnosis?
questions.exp: AFP is raised in AT.

questions.question: A child has morning headaches, vomiting, truncal ataxia and nystagmus. What is the most likely tumour?
questions.exp: Medulloblastoma is a midline posterior fossa tumour causing truncal ataxia and hydrocephalus.

questions.question: Which condition causes a false negative Mantoux test?
questions.exp: Malnutrition and immunosuppression blunt the response.

questions.question: Which condition causes a false negative sweat chloride test?
questions.exp: Oedema lowers sweat chloride.

questions.question: A child has fever with arthritis of the knee that moves to the elbow. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Migratory polyarthritis of large joints is a major Jones criterion.

questions.question: A doctor interrupts a nurse and does not let her contribute. Which principle is breached?
questions.exp: Fair and respectful team processes.
questions.d: Procedural justice and respect for colleagues

questions.question: A 7-year-old has typical absence seizures. Ethosuximide is not offered. Which drug is appropriate?
questions.exp: Ethosuximide or valproate are first-line; carbamazepine and phenytoin worsen absences.

questions.question: Which condition is associated with optic nerve glioma?
questions.exp: Optic pathway gliomas in NF1.

questions.question: How is Tourette syndrome diagnosed?
questions.exp: Multiple motor and at least one vocal tic for more than a year.

questions.question: Which drug can be used for severe tics in Tourette syndrome?
questions.exp: Alpha-agonists and antipsychotics are used. The recall writer chose haloperidol.
questions.d: Clonidine or an antipsychotic such as haloperidol

questions.question: A 4-year-old stutters at times when excited. What is the advice?
questions.exp: Developmental dysfluency is common at 2-5 years; refer if persistent or distressing.

questions.question: A 4-year-old shows jealousy and aggression towards his new baby sibling. What is the advice?
questions.exp: Give individual attention and involve the child in caring for the baby.
questions.d: Behaviour modification with special time and praise

questions.question: A 6-year-old starts bedwetting after the family moves house. What is the first approach?
questions.exp: Secondary enuresis related to stress usually settles; positive reinforcement and checking for UTI and diabetes.
questions.a: Reassure with a reward system (star chart)

questions.question: What is a common mechanism of primary nocturnal enuresis?
questions.exp: Mismatch between nocturnal urine output, bladder capacity and arousal. The recall writer chose decreased bladder capacity.
questions.a: Nocturnal polyuria, reduced bladder capacity or failure to wake

questions.question: A 2-year-old says only "mama" and "dada". What is the first investigation?
questions.exp: Hearing should be assessed in any child with speech delay.

questions.question: A child has a brain abscess on CT. What is the empirical treatment?
questions.exp: Covers streptococci, staphylococci and anaerobes.

questions.question: A child has abdominal pain and retching without vomiting; contrast stops at the pylorus and an NG tube cannot be passed. What is the management?
questions.exp: Retching without vomiting and failure to pass an NG tube (Borchardt triad) suggest gastric volvulus, a surgical emergency.

questions.question: A child has abdominal pain and retching without vomiting, and an NG tube cannot be passed. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Borchardt triad: pain, unproductive retching and inability to pass an NG tube. The recall writer suggested a foreign body at the pylorus.

questions.question: An infant sits, crawls and has a palmar grasp but no pincer grasp. What is the developmental age?
questions.exp: Crawling and sitting at 8-9 months; the pincer grasp appears at 9-10 months. The recall writer chose 13-14 months.

questions.question: What is the most common organism causing infective endocarditis in children?
questions.exp: Viridans streptococci, then Staph aureus.

questions.question: A mother refuses lumbar puncture for her stable child after full explanation. What should be done?
questions.exp: Parental refusal of a non-life-saving test is respected; treat empirically.
questions.c: Respect her refusal, document, and treat empirically

questions.question: A mother refuses a routine vaccine after counselling. What should the doctor do?
questions.exp: Policy varies; in Saudi Arabia vaccination is mandatory, so authorities may be informed.
questions.b: Document the refusal and follow local policy (inform public health if mandated)

questions.question: A drug company offers a doctor pens with its logo. What should the doctor do?
questions.exp: Gifts from industry, even small ones, should be avoided.
questions.b: Accept if he likes the drug

questions.question: A doctor sends his patients to his own medical equipment business. What is this?
questions.exp: Self-referral for financial gain is a conflict of interest.

questions.question: A consultant teaches a student to always tell patients accurate information. Which principle is this?
questions.exp: Veracity is truthfulness; fidelity is keeping promises.

questions.question: A child speaks in sentences, names 4 colours and hops. What is the developmental age?
questions.exp: Names colours and hops on one foot at 4 years.

questions.question: A child has oral vesicles, vesicles on the toes and diarrhoea. What is the management?
questions.exp: HFMD is self-limiting. The recall writer chose acyclovir.

questions.question: A child with nasal decongestant overdose has severe narrow-complex tachycardia and is stable. What is the treatment?
questions.exp: Vagal manoeuvres then adenosine for stable SVT.

questions.question: A child has SVT at 300/min with hypotension and prolonged capillary refill. What is the treatment?
questions.exp: Unstable SVT: synchronised cardioversion 0.5-1 J/kg (adenosine if IV access is immediate).

questions.question: A girl cannot comb her hair or climb stairs and has red papules over the knuckles. What is the most useful test?
questions.exp: Gottron papules with proximal weakness; CK is raised.

questions.question: Which complication of Raynaud phenomenon occurs in scleroderma?
questions.exp: Severe vasospasm leads to digital ischaemia.

questions.question: A newborn has a skin-covered occipital swelling containing brain tissue. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Neural tube defect of the skull.

questions.question: A child has a generalised maculopapular rash after cough, coryza and conjunctivitis, with a neighbour who had a similar illness. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Prodrome of the 3 Cs, Koplik spots, then rash from the head down.

questions.question: What is the treatment of acute otitis media needing antibiotics?
questions.exp: High-dose amoxicillin covers resistant pneumococcus.

questions.question: A child with otitis media becomes irritable and drowsy. What is the next step?
questions.exp: Meningitis is a complication of otitis media.

questions.question: A toddler took an unknown drug and has pinpoint pupils, bradycardia, hypotension and drowsiness. What is the most likely drug?
questions.exp: Clonidine mimics opioid toxidrome with bradycardia and hypotension.

questions.question: A neonate after exchange transfusion via an umbilical venous catheter has haematuria and a flank mass. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Catheters, dehydration and polycythaemia predispose.

questions.question: A neonate has haematuria and a flank mass. What is the investigation?
questions.exp: Doppler shows absent venous flow.

questions.question: A virilised female neonate has low sodium and high potassium. What is the diagnostic test?
questions.exp: 21-hydroxylase deficiency raises 17-OHP.

questions.question: A 3-day-old has abdominal distension with milky then bilious vomiting; rectal examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bilious vomiting needs urgent upper GI contrast.

questions.question: A neonate with suspected midgut volvulus is stable. What is the management?
questions.exp: Unstable infants go straight to theatre.
questions.d: NG decompression, IV fluids and urgent upper GI contrast

questions.question: A neonate passed meconium on day 3 and there is an explosive gush of stool after rectal examination. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Confirm with rectal suction biopsy.

questions.question: A child after Hirschsprung pull-through has fever, abdominal distension and foul diarrhoea. What is the management?
questions.exp: Enterocolitis is the main cause of death; treat with washouts, IV fluids and antibiotics.
questions.c: Rectal washouts with warm saline plus IV antibiotics

questions.question: A child in DKA has potassium 2.5 mmol/L. What should be done?
questions.exp: Insulin drives potassium into cells; correct severe hypokalaemia first. The recall writer chose 40 mEq KCl plus potassium phosphate.
questions.b: Add potassium 40 mmol/L to fluids and delay insulin until K is above 3.5

questions.question: A child has platelets 140, giant platelets on film and absent aggregation with ristocetin, with normal von Willebrand factor. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bernard-Soulier (GPIb deficiency): giant platelets, mild thrombocytopenia, no ristocetin aggregation. Glanzmann has normal platelet counts and ristocetin response.

questions.question: A boy with severe haemophilia A has a haemarthrosis and a low-titre inhibitor (2 BU). What is the treatment?
questions.exp: Low-titre inhibitors (< 5 BU) can be overcome with high-dose FVIII; high-titre needs bypassing agents (rFVIIa).

questions.question: A child has short stature, a high-pitched voice, truncal adiposity and a doll-like face. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: GH deficiency causes immature facies, high-pitched voice and micropenis.

questions.question: What is the treatment of growth hormone deficiency?
questions.exp: Daily subcutaneous GH.

questions.question: A child on peritoneal dialysis has fever, abdominal pain and cloudy dialysate. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Effluent WBC > 100/µL with > 50% neutrophils; treat with intraperitoneal antibiotics.

questions.question: A 2-month-old has Hb 9 g/dL with normal MCV and is well. What is the management?
questions.exp: Physiological nadir.

questions.question: A child with ALL in neutropenia has pyoderma. What is the empirical treatment?
questions.exp: Febrile neutropenia needs broad anti-pseudomonal cover; skin infection may need gram-positive cover.
questions.a: Piperacillin-tazobactam plus gentamicin (add vancomycin if MRSA suspected)

questions.question: A child with ALL has fever and an infected central venous line. What is the empirical treatment?
questions.exp: Line infection adds coagulase-negative staph and MRSA cover.

questions.question: An obese child on lifestyle changes still has high cholesterol and triglycerides. What is next?
questions.exp: Statins from 8-10 years if LDL remains high after lifestyle measures.
questions.c: Continue diet and consider a statin

questions.question: A child has facial swelling, breathlessness, basal crackles, hepatomegaly and hypertension 2 weeks after a URTI. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Fluid overload with hypertension and haematuria; low C3.

questions.question: What is an early sign of septic shock in children?
questions.exp: Tachycardia is early; hypotension is late.

questions.question: What protection is needed for airborne infections such as TB?
questions.exp: Airborne precautions: N95 and negative-pressure room.

questions.question: What protection is needed for droplet infections such as influenza?
questions.exp: Droplet precautions: surgical mask within 1-2 m.

questions.question: A 7-month-old with recurrent febrile UTIs has another infection. Which investigation looks for the cause?
questions.exp: MCUG diagnoses vesicoureteral reflux; DMSA detects scarring.

questions.question: Which factor is cryoprecipitate rich in?
questions.exp: Cryo contains fibrinogen, FVIII, vWF and FXIII.

questions.question: Where should a new children's hospital be built?
questions.exp: Planning should match services to population need.
questions.c: In the area with the most children needing care

questions.question: An infant has fever, cough and runny nose with family members who have colds, and worsens over 2 days. What is the most likely organism?
questions.exp: RSV bronchiolitis peaks at day 3-5.

questions.question: After an arterial switch for transposition, which ECG problem is more associated with the older atrial switch?
questions.exp: Atrial switch (Mustard/Senning) causes sinus node dysfunction; the arterial switch causes coronary problems.

questions.question: An immunocompromised child is exposed to varicella. What should be given?
questions.exp: VZIG within 10 days of exposure.

questions.question: A child has peaked T waves on ECG with hyperkalaemia. What is the first treatment?
questions.exp: Calcium stabilises the myocardium; then insulin-glucose and salbutamol.

questions.question: A child with tricyclic antidepressant poisoning has wide QRS. What is the antidote?
questions.exp: Sodium bicarbonate treats QRS widening and arrhythmias. The recall writer's keyed answer of atropine is not standard.

questions.question: What is a poor prognostic sign in tricyclic antidepressant overdose?
questions.exp: QRS width predicts seizures and arrhythmias; hypotension predicts mortality.

questions.question: A child with pneumonia worsens with sudden breathlessness and a hyper-resonant percussion note. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Hyper-resonance with reduced breath sounds.

questions.question: A 2-week-old breastfed baby has unconjugated jaundice and is well. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Prolonged unconjugated jaundice in a thriving breastfed baby; still check thyroid and conjugated level.

questions.question: A child has painless maroon stools and anaemia. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Ectopic gastric mucosa ulcerates; technetium scan confirms.

questions.question: A newborn has a coiled NG tube on X-ray and a gasless abdomen. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: No gas in the abdomen means no distal fistula.

questions.question: A 6-year-old has right upper lobe consolidation with gradual onset, headache and dry cough. What is the treatment?
questions.exp: Atypical features at school age suggest Mycoplasma; macrolides. Typical lobar pneumonia needs amoxicillin. Details were partly reconstructed.

questions.question: A 9-month-old admitted with gastroenteritis has head lag. What should be done?
questions.exp: Head lag at 9 months is abnormal but may reflect illness; reassess when well.

questions.question: A 13-year-old has recurrent abdominal pain and difficulty swallowing with normal investigations. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Functional symptoms with normal tests; look for psychosocial stress.

questions.question: A child has failure to thrive, polyuria, polydipsia, normal BP, hypokalaemia, hypochloraemia and metabolic alkalosis. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Normal BP excludes hyperaldosteronism and Liddle.

questions.question: What is the investigation for suspected choanal atresia?
questions.exp: Fine-cut CT shows bony or membranous obstruction.

questions.question: What is the most common type of choanal atresia?
questions.exp: About 70% mixed.

questions.question: A child has a nasal "polyp" seen on examination. What should be done before any biopsy?
questions.exp: A midline nasal mass in a child may be an encephalocele or glioma.
questions.d: MRI or CT to exclude encephalocele

questions.question: A short girl had menarche at 10.5 years. What explains her short adult height?
questions.exp: Early fusion limits final height.
questions.a: Early puberty with early growth plate fusion

questions.question: Which urine finding is typical of pre-renal azotaemia?
questions.exp: Pre-renal: urine osmolality > 500, Na < 20, FENa < 1%.
questions.b: Concentrated urine with high specific gravity and low urine sodium

questions.question: A child aspirates a peanut, becomes cyanosed then pink. Where is the peanut most likely to be?
questions.exp: The right main bronchus is wider and more vertical.

questions.question: A mother with a malar rash has a newborn with bradycardia. What does the ECG show?
questions.exp: Maternal anti-Ro/La antibodies damage the conduction system.

questions.question: After liver transplant a child has jaundice and is HBsAg positive. What is the next investigation?
questions.exp: Biopsy distinguishes rejection from recurrent viral hepatitis. The recall writer chose biopsy.

questions.question: A 12-year-old with height 115 cm has an ejection systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to the neck. What is the lesion?
questions.exp: Williams syndrome with short stature.

questions.question: A child has acute asthma. What is the first-line treatment?
questions.exp: Salbutamol via spacer or nebuliser.

questions.question: An asthmatic child has more attacks in winter. What advice is given?
questions.exp: Influenza triggers attacks.

questions.question: Which vaccines should be given to a child with HIV?
questions.exp: Avoid live vaccines in severe immunosuppression.
questions.a: Inactivated vaccines such as DTaP and pneumococcal
questions.c: Yellow fever if CD4 is low

questions.question: A 6-month-old had anaphylaxis after 4-month vaccines. What is next?
questions.exp: Identify the culprit component.

questions.question: A junior diagnoses UTI; before treatment is started the senior reviews and says it is not a UTI. What is this event?
questions.exp: An error caught before reaching the patient is a near miss.

questions.question: What is the management of frequent sleepwalking at a predictable time?
questions.exp: Scheduled awakenings and safety measures.
questions.c: Scheduled awakening 15-30 minutes before the usual episode

questions.question: A 2-month-old has tachycardia, poor feeding and hepatomegaly. Which lesion is most likely?
questions.exp: Large VSDs cause heart failure at 6-8 weeks as pulmonary resistance falls.

questions.question: When should a large VSD with pulmonary hypertension be repaired?
questions.exp: Early repair prevents irreversible pulmonary vascular disease. The recall writer chose 6-12 months.

questions.question: A teenager has bone pain and a sunburst periosteal reaction on X-ray. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Sunburst and Codman triangle at the metaphysis; Ewing gives onion-skin.

questions.question: An infant with VSD on captopril, furosemide and digoxin still has heart failure and a palpable P2. What is next?
questions.exp: Failure of medical treatment with pulmonary hypertension needs surgery.

questions.question: A child with dark skin pigmentation and pancytopenia is assessed. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Café-au-lait, short stature, thumb anomalies, marrow failure.

questions.question: A child has wide fixed splitting of S2. What is the lesion?
questions.exp: Increased RV volume delays pulmonary closure.

questions.question: A child has fever, stridor and drooling. What is the initial management?
questions.exp: Avoid upsetting the child. The recall writer chose nasotracheal intubation.
questions.a: Keep calm and secure the airway in theatre by an experienced team

questions.question: Which condition needs special care during examination?
questions.exp: Do not examine the throat; may cause complete obstruction.

questions.question: A child has intestinal obstruction with multiple air-fluid levels. What indicates surgical referral?
questions.exp: Multiple air-fluid levels with distension and bilious vomiting need surgery.
questions.d: The X-ray findings with signs of obstruction

questions.question: An antenatal scan shows a cystic lung lesion. What is the investigation after birth?
questions.exp: CT defines CPAM or sequestration even if the baby is well.

questions.question: A child who eats junk food and watches a lot of TV has constipation with impacted stool. What is the first step?
questions.exp: Disimpaction, then maintenance laxatives and diet.
